{{short description|Positional game}}
{{one source|date=January 2019}}

In [[combinatorial game theory]], an '''arithmetic progression game''' is a [[positional game]] where two players alternately pick numbers, trying to occupy a complete [[arithmetic progression]] of a given size.

The game is parameterized by two integers <math>n>k</math>. The game-board is the set <math>\{1,\dots,n\}</math>. The winning-sets are all the arithmetic progressions of length <math>k</math>.   In a [[Maker-Breaker game]] variant, the first player (Maker) wins by occupying a <math>k</math>-length arithmetic progression, otherwise the second player (Breaker) wins.

The game is also called the '''van der Waerden game''',<ref name="beck81">{{Cite journal|last=Beck|first=József|date=1981|title=Van der Waerden and Ramsey type games|journal=Combinatorica|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=103–116|doi=10.1007/bf02579267|issn=0209-9683}}</ref>  named after [[Van der Waerden's theorem]]. It says that, for any <math>k</math>, there exists some integer <math>W(2,k)</math> such that, if the integers <math>\{1, \dots,W(2,k)</math> are partitioned arbitrarily into two sets, then at least one set contains an arithmetic progression of length <math>k</math>.  This means that,  if <math>n \geq W(2,k)</math>, then Maker has a winning strategy.

This claim is not constructive - it does not show a specific strategy for Maker. Moreover, the current upper bound for <math>W(2,k)</math> is extremely large: the currently known bounds are
<math display=block>2^{k}/k^\varepsilon < W(2,k) < 2^{2^{2^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}}</math>
for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>.

Let <math>W^*(2,k)</math> be the smallest integer such that Maker has a winning strategy.  [[József Beck|Beck]]<ref name="beck81" /> proves that <math>2^{k-7k^{7/8}} < W^*(2,k) < k^3 2^{k-4}</math>. In particular, if  <math>k^3 2^{k-4} < n</math>, then the game is Maker's win (even though it is much smaller than the number that guarantees no-draw).
